- Model consistently overestimates prices, especially in early forecast periods (first 5–10 days of 30d window).
- Forecasts show a strong upward trend bias, often peaking too early and then declining too sharply — suggesting failure to capture mean reversion or volatility clustering.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., 90s to 97s), model underreacts to subsequent drops, failing to adjust downward quickly enough.
- Model tends to underestimate true price volatility, particularly in mid-to-late forecast horizon (days 15–30), leading to overly smooth or flat trajectories.
- Forecasts often lag behind true price movements by 1–3 days, especially in downward trends — model reacts too slowly to market corrections.
- In cases of sustained high prices, model fails to anticipate sharp downward corrections, leading to over-optimistic forecasts.
- Model exhibits “overshoot” behavior after price spikes — forecasts peak higher than true price, then drop faster than reality, suggesting poor calibration to volatility decay.
- Forecasts are overly optimistic in the first 5–7 days, then gradually flatten — suggesting model doesn’t account for short-term momentum decay or policy-driven volatility.
- In low-price regimes (e.g., 80s), model tends to underestimate true price drops, leading to persistent overestimation of stability.
- Model fails to capture “mean reversion” in price clusters — often forecasts remain flat when true prices exhibit strong oscillation or correction patterns.
